title: AI-powered camera system offers low-cost way to monitor bumblebees, potentially other insects
excerpt: Researchers have developed a low-cost, semi-automated, AI-driven method that uses remote cameras to survey bumblebees and potentially other insects. The new tool could have important implications for efforts to conserve declining insect populations. Several bumblebee species have been petitioned to be listed under the Endangered Species Act.
content_html:
Researchers have developed a low-cost, semi-automated, AI-driven method that uses remote cameras to survey bumblebees and potentially other insects. The new tool could have important implications for efforts to conserve declining insect populations. Several bumblebee species have been petitioned to be listed under the Endangered Species Act.

Researchers also say the technology could benefit agriculture, given that many crops depend on insects as pollinators.

"Insects are vitally important, and we need methods to better understand their populations," said Michael Getz, a data scientist at Biodiversity Research Institute in Maine, who led this research as a master's student at Oregon State University. "This tool should help us to do that in a low-cost, easily scalable manner."

The findings were published in the journal Remote Sensing in Ecology and Conservation.

Traditional insect surveys typically rely on one of two methods, both of which have drawbacks. Traps are often used, but they are lethal to the insects. Direct observation, often involving insect nets, is labor-intensive, time-consuming and costly.

The Oregon State research team built on recent studies showing trail cameras can capture images of insects in a noninvasive manner. Most previous work, however, focused on nocturnal insects such as moths, which can easily be attracted to cameras using light.

Less was known about how to attract and monitor diurnal insects, which are active in daylight. The researchers sought to determine the most effective way to lure bumblebees to camera stations, identify them automatically once photographed and compare camera-based monitoring with conventional survey techniques.

To accomplish this, the researchers built an inexpensive camera system using commercially available components and deployed it during bloom in a red clover seed field at Oregon State's Hyslop Field Research Laboratory in Corvallis.

Alongside the cameras, researchers surveyed bumblebees using hand-netting and blue vane traps, tools used by researchers to attract insects that are deadly to bees. The camera system recorded six bumblebee species and closely matched the diversity of species documented through netting and traps.

To identify the bumblebee images, they fed the images into two types of custom-built deep-learning image-analysis models. They found that tiled models, which divide images into smaller sections and analyze each segment individually, outperformed models that evaluated entire images at once.

The researchers also tested several visual patterns placed behind the cameras to attract bumblebees and found bullseye patterns drew significantly more bee visits than uniform-colored backgrounds.

"One of the biggest challenges in understanding pollinator health and ecology is collecting enough information across large landscapes," said Tim Warren, an assistant professor in the Oregon State Department of Horticulture. "These results show that we can gather reliable data with camera systems like this and begin to understand population and movement trends at a scale that hasn't been practical before."

The ability to generate large-scale monitoring data is especially valuable as more bumblebee species are evaluated for federal protection, said Andony Melathopoulos, a co-author of the paper and an associate professor of pollinator health at Oregon State.

Data gaps often complicate decisions about whether species should be listed under the Endangered Species Act and how critical habitat should be designated, he said.

"This technology opens up the possibility for much richer data so that we can be more precise when it comes to decisions on listing a species and characterizing critical habitat," Melathopoulos said.

Other co-authors of the paper are Lincoln Best, a bee taxonomist at Oregon State, and Oksana Ostroverkhova, a physics professor at Oregon State.

content_html_zh:
研究人员开发了一种低成本、半自动化、人工智能驱动的方法，使用远程摄像头来调查大黄蜂和其他潜在昆虫。 新工具可能对保护不断减少的昆虫种群的努力产生重要影响。 一些熊蜂物种已被请求列入《濒危物种法》。

研究人员还表示，鉴于许多作物依赖昆虫作为传粉者，这项技术可能使农业受益。

缅因州生物多样性研究所的数据科学家迈克尔·盖兹（Michael Getz）在俄勒冈州立大学担任硕士生时领导了这项研究，他说：“昆虫至关重要，我们需要方法来更好地了解它们的种群。” “这个工具应该帮助我们以低成本、易于扩展的方式做到这一点。”

研究结果发表在《生态与保护遥感》杂志上。

传统的昆虫调查通常依赖两种方法之一，这两种方法都有缺点。 经常使用陷阱，但它们对昆虫来说是致命的。 直接观察通常需要使用防虫网，这是一项劳动密集型、耗时且昂贵的工作。

俄勒冈州立大学的研究小组最近的研究表明，追踪相机可以以非侵入性的方式捕捉昆虫的图像。 然而，之前的大多数工作都集中在夜行动物上，例如飞蛾，它们很容易被光线吸引到相机上。

人们对如何吸引和监测白天活动的昆虫知之甚少。 研究人员试图确定将大黄蜂引诱到摄像站的最有效方法，在拍摄后自动识别它们，并将基于摄像头的监测与传统的调查技术进行比较。

为了实现这一目标，研究人员使用市售组件构建了一个廉价的摄像系统，并在开花期间将其部署在俄勒冈州科瓦利斯希斯洛普田间研究实验室的红三叶草种子田中。

除了摄像机之外，研究人员还使用手网和蓝色叶片陷阱对大黄蜂进行了调查，这些工具是研究人员用来吸引对蜜蜂致命的昆虫的。 摄像系统记录了六种大黄蜂物种，并且与通过网和陷阱记录的物种多样性非常匹配。

为了识别大黄蜂图像，他们将图像输入两种类型的定制深度学习图像分析模型。 他们发现平铺模型将图像分成更小的部分并单独分析每个部分，其性能优于同时评估整个图像的模型。

研究人员还测试了放置在摄像机后面的几种吸引大黄蜂的视觉图案，发现靶心图案比均匀颜色的背景吸引的蜜蜂数量明显更多。

俄勒冈州园艺部助理教授蒂姆·沃伦说：“了解传粉媒介健康和生态的最大挑战之一是在大片景观中收集足够的信息。” “这些结果表明，我们可以使用这样的摄像系统收集可靠的数据，并开始以前所未有的规模了解人口和流动趋势。”

该论文的合著者、俄勒冈州立大学传粉昆虫健康副教授安东尼·梅拉索普洛斯 (Andony Melathopoulos) 表示，随着越来越多的熊蜂物种接受联邦保护评估，生成大规模监测数据的能力尤其有价值。

他说，数据差距常常使有关物种是否应列入《濒危物种法》以及如何指定关键栖息地的决策变得复杂。

梅拉索普洛斯说：“这项技术为获得更丰富的数据提供了可能性，以便我们在列出物种和描述关键栖息地的决策时能够更加精确。”

这篇论文的其他合著者包括俄勒冈州立大学的蜜蜂分类学家林肯·贝斯特（Lincoln Best）和俄勒冈州立大学的物理学教授奥克萨娜·奥斯特罗弗科娃（Oksana Ostroverkhova）。
